public_rationale: The Apple study supports the ordinary reliability claim: its models failed at exact algorithm execution, including when given the algorithm. That makes them unsuitable as general replacements under those conditions. This does not establish that no LLM can ever substitute on any task. Follow-up studies and MAKER materially limit that stronger interpretation.
limitations: The conclusion concerns the original experimental setting.
The outcome depends on reading no substitute as a general reliability claim, rather than a universal impossibility claim.
Later successful systems used materially different execution arrangements.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: LLMs are no substitute for good, well-specified conventional algorithms.

statement.excerpt: What the Apple paper shows, most fundamentally, regardless of how you define AGI, is that LLMs are no substitute for good well-specified conventional algorithms.
statement.document_title: Even more good news for the future of neurosymbolic AI

our_interpretation: The plain reading is that LLM-generated answers cannot generally replace reliable execution of specified algorithms when correctness matters.
The statement explicitly describes what the Apple study demonstrated. The target period is its June 2025 reporting period, rather than all subsequent model development.
Writing or calling conventional software is different from replacing its execution with model-generated steps.
This does not mean that LLMs cannot solve any algorithmic problem.
criteria.support_condition: The study documents systematic failures to execute specified, solvable algorithms correctly as task size increases.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable evaluations show the tested models reliably executing the specified algorithms across the tested sizes, or establish that the reported failures disappear after correcting material experimental errors.

evidence.explanation: The study reports failures even when an explicit algorithm is supplied. This supports the limited conclusion that the tested models were not reliable general replacements for algorithm execution.

This follow-up reports substantially better River Crossing results under revised conditions, while retaining Hanoi difficulties. It cautions against treating every original failure as a general reasoning limit.

evidence.locator: Abstract; sections 3 and 4 describe the method and experiment
evidence.explanation: MAKER reports completing a 20-disk Hanoi task with over one million steps and no errors. Its decomposition and voting machinery shows why the Apple findings should not be extended to every LLM-based system.
